channel.title: Vikram Chopra
channel.description: I am the founder of Cars24. These essays are the worldview underneath it: how a country learns to own cars, why trust is the real product in mobility, what a company becomes when AI collapses the cost of coordination, and how a builder stays clear-eyed while the stakes rise.

item.title: Before You Call Someone Careless
item.description: We often explain our own behavior with context and other people's with character. That shortcut can make us miss the pressures and conditions that shaped what happened.
item.content:encoded:
You had reasons. They had flaws.

That is how the mistake can feel from the inside. One easy mistake is to believe that behavior explains itself. Someone is sharp in a meeting, and we decide they are arrogant. Someone misses a deadline, and we decide they are careless. Someone cuts us off in traffic, and we decide they are reckless.

We take a moment and turn it into a judgment about a person. The move is so quick that it does not feel like interpretation. It feels like perception. But behavior does not happen in isolation. It happens under pressure and inside a situation. Sometimes we are seeing a person collide with context we do not understand.

Two moral systems

Psychologists gave this tendency a name. In 1977, Lee Ross described the fundamental attribution error: our tendency to explain other people's behavior through their character while giving too little weight to their situation.

A few years earlier, Edward Jones and Richard Nisbett described a related pattern called the actor-observer asymmetry. We explain our own actions through circumstance and other people's actions through character. When someone else behaves badly, we may call them lazy, difficult, or selfish. When we behave badly, we may say we were exhausted, under pressure, or working with poor information. The double standard is obvious on paper and nearly invisible while we live it. We do not feel as if we are using two moral systems. We feel as if we are being accurate. Other people start to look simpler than they are, while we give ourselves the more complete story.

I catch myself doing this more than I would like. As a founder, it is easy to call someone careless when I did not manage them well, or to call a team slow when I had not made the priorities clear. I have been on the other side too. People inside my company have read my shifting priorities as impulsiveness, as evidence that I cannot hold a belief. From inside my head, the shifts are part of one connected line of thought. They see character. I see circumstance. We can both make the mistake this essay describes. The character story is always available, and it tends to flatter the person telling it.

One reason the bias can persist is that explanations about character feel clean. If someone disappoints us, it is simpler to decide they are unreliable than to hold a more complicated picture. Character stories give us a quick sense of closure. That speed can be useful, but it can also mislead us. Human behavior rarely has only one cause. Someone may be careless, and also exhausted, poorly managed, or afraid to raise a concern. The behavior may be real while our explanation for it is wrong. When the explanation hardens too quickly, we stop investigating. Premature certainty is the danger.

Context deepens the diagnosis

This is where people can get uncomfortable. They hear an emphasis on situation and assume it means going soft. It does not. Context does not erase responsibility. It can make the diagnosis more complete.

If a person in authority humiliates someone publicly, we still need to address what they did. It may also matter whether the environment normalized aggression and rewarded fear-based speed. If a frontline employee seems disengaged, their behavior matters. So might the conditions of a punishing role or incentives that work against one another. A person remains responsible for their actions, but a fuller explanation can help us choose a useful response.

Shallow diagnosis is one source of recurring failure in families, teams, and institutions. A company sees poor execution and calls someone weak instead of asking whether the system is creating confusion. We can find it easier to condemn a person than to understand the conditions around them.

This is not a case for naivety. Behavior is evidence. Actions can tell us something about a person, and some people are as careless or cruel as they appear. The point is that a moment is evidence, not the whole case. The deeper cost of getting this wrong is that we become less able to hold complexity. Once we are attached to a character story, we may start selecting evidence that confirms it. A colleague who had a bad season becomes the kind of person who always does this. A family member under strain becomes impossible. Moral simplification is tempting because it is efficient. It can also make us worse at understanding people.

Accuracy over the easy story

The fix is not to eliminate a bias we may not be able to eliminate. It is to interrupt it before it hardens, by asking better questions. What else might explain this? What pressure might this person be under that I cannot see? If I had behaved this way, what situational explanation would I give myself? Am I seeing a pattern, or moralizing one moment?

Those questions make a judgment more careful. The point is not niceness. It is accuracy. We can hold people accountable and still ask what shaped their actions. Strong standards need a good understanding of causes. If we misread the cause, our intervention can become theater. We punish when the system needs redesign, or coach when a boundary is needed.

There is a human truth underneath this. Most of us have acted in ways that did not reflect who we want to be. Taken out of context, those moments can make us look smaller or colder than the fuller story. We know this about ourselves and can forget to extend the same curiosity to other people.

People may be tired, afraid, badly managed, or working inside systems that reward the wrong behavior. Someone else may judge them by character because that is easier to see than context. When we do that too often, we become less fair and less accurate. If we want to judge or work with people well, accuracy matters more than the comfort of a quick conclusion.

I do this too. I give myself reasons and other people flaws. The work is to catch the sentence before it hardens.

Notes and Sources

  • Lee Ross, “The Intuitive Psychologist and His Shortcomings,” Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 1977. The fundamental attribution error.
  • Edward Jones and Richard Nisbett, “The Actor and the Observer: Divergent Perceptions of the Causes of Behavior,” 1971. The actor-observer asymmetry.

item.title: The Conversation Before the Postmortem
item.description: Delay and weak accountability often show up as process problems. Some begin earlier, when people do not trust one another enough to speak plainly or commit to a decision.
item.content:encoded:
Many execution reviews start too late. By the time a launch has slipped, the failure may have begun in a quieter room. Someone did not say what they knew. Someone nodded without committing. Someone took a disagreement upward instead of raising it with a peer.

The postmortem then sounds familiar: planning, ownership, follow-through, process. Those may be the right things to examine. Sometimes, though, they describe where the problem surfaced rather than where it began. The harder question is whether people trusted one another enough to speak plainly and early. That shifts the conversation from procedure to fear, avoidance, politeness, and the desire to be liked instead of clear.

This is why Patrick Lencioni's The Five Dysfunctions of a Team has endured. It names a pattern many teams recognize: low trust can make people avoid conflict. Without useful conflict, people may leave a discussion without a real commitment. That weakens accountability and can eventually affect results. The model is useful because the dashboard is late. By the time a metric turns red, the team may have spent weeks avoiding the conversation that would have helped explain it.

Where the miss usually hides

Many companies can recite the model. Fewer notice where they stop short of using it. In my experience, the real work often hides in three places.

Process language feels safer. If a launch slipped because the weekly review was weak, you can fix the weekly review. If it slipped because two people did not trust one another enough to disagree three weeks earlier, the problem gets personal. Then you have to ask whether people hide disagreement until it becomes expensive, whether meetings are for making decisions or performing politeness, and whether the team prefers false peace to useful friction.

That is a more uncomfortable diagnosis, so organizations can keep repairing the visible machinery while leaving the human structure untouched. Artificial harmony is costly. From the outside, it can look mature: polite meetings, few flare-ups, and apparent alignment. Then the real discussion starts after the meeting, in side conversations and private reservations. People comply without committing. What looks like an execution problem may be an honesty problem. Healthy conflict costs something in the moment and can save time later. Avoiding conflict feels cheap at first and can become expensive.

Commitment is not consensus. Teams often confuse the two. Real commitment does not require everyone to get the outcome they preferred. People need a clear decision and a chance to be heard. Once the debate is over, they need enough clarity to act on the decision, even if it was not their first choice.

Many teams never get there. They leave with phrases like roughly aligned or let's refine as we go. Those words can sound collaborative while leaving the decision unclear. That ambiguity travels downstream as flexibility. I am wary of cultures that treat consensus as the only fair outcome. They can leave people less ready to act because nobody has said plainly what the decision is or who owns the next step.

Accountability is hard among peers. Teams can treat accountability as a manager's job. A stronger team also makes room for colleagues to speak directly when standards slip. That can be awkward, so people may escalate upward or soften feedback until it changes nothing. Then the manager becomes the only source of correction. If people can only say the hard thing to someone with formal authority, the team still has work to do on candor and peer accountability.

Process still matters. Clear roles, decision rights, and review rhythms help people work together. But process depends on the quality of the conversations underneath it. A team with little trust can turn any process into bureaucracy. A team that avoids conflict can turn any meeting rhythm into theater. Amy Edmondson's work on psychological safety points to one condition that helps: people are more able to raise concerns and admit mistakes when doing so does not expose them to humiliation. Without that, an operating system can run on incomplete information.

The exception I live

Here is where I have to push beyond the model. I have caught myself avoiding hard conversations with my own co-founders, even though we have built a great deal of trust. We have spent more than a decade together. Time has worn down some of our egos. We know one another's intentions. By the model, candor should feel easy for us. It does not. There can still be a pause before the sentence, and butterflies.

Kim Scott tells a story from the other side. After fifteen years of working with people who trusted and liked her, someone finally told her about the metaphorical spinach in her teeth. Trust gave people a reason to care about the relationship. It did not mean the difficult feedback happened by itself.

That has changed how I think about candor. Trust is a foundation, but it is not the skill. You can believe that feedback and bad news are gifts, and still fail to say the hard thing. Practice helps. The butterflies may simply be part of the moment. I now try to treat candor as a rep to do, not a trait to assume. A team that waits to feel comfortable before being honest may wait a long time. Comfort is not the precondition. It may come after the practice.

Many execution problems do not begin with execution. Some begin with concerns people have not made clear to one another. The answer is not always another review meeting. We need a room where people can speak honestly, early enough for the review meeting to have something true to work with.

Notes and Sources

  • Patrick Lencioni, The Five Dysfunctions of a Team, 2002. The trust-to-results chain.
  • Amy Edmondson, “Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams,” Administrative Science Quarterly, 1999. Research on psychological safety and learning behavior in teams.
  • Kim Scott, Radical Candor, 2017. The story about feedback that went unspoken for fifteen years.

item.title: Who Taught You to Want This?
item.description: Much of what we call ambition is shaped by peers, rivals, and status systems before we recognize their influence. Asking where a desire came from can help us choose what to pursue.
item.content:encoded:
For a long time, I thought desire was one of the most private things about a person. What you want, what you chase, and what kind of life feels meaningful can seem deeply personal.

Then you watch people closely, including yourself, and the picture gets stranger. Why do so many people end up wanting the same things? Why can satisfaction fade, not because life got worse, but because somebody nearby got something you thought you should have had? Some of what we call desire is less original than we like to believe. Much of it is learned from other people.

Desire is social

This is not a new observation. The French thinker René Girard built his work around mimetic desire: the idea that we learn what to want by watching other people. We often speak about desire as if it rises from deep inside us. Find your passion. Know what you want. Ignore the noise. That advice assumes there is a pure personal signal waiting underneath the confusion.

Real life feels less clean. We learn what is desirable by watching what other people value. We copy taste before we know we are copying it, and we take on ambitions before noticing where they came from. That does not make desire fake. It means desire is social, which is more uncomfortable. Some of our strongest ambitions may already be shaped by the people around us. So the question is not only what you want. It is also who taught you to want it.

People often assume desire is distorted by celebrities. That happens, but closer models can have a stronger effect. Girard distinguished a distant model, who can inspire fantasy, from a close model, who can become a rival. A billionaire in another country may be a spectacle. A founder from your batch raising more capital than you can feel like a wound. A friend buying the house you thought you should be able to buy can make you restless.

Luke Burgis, who brought Girard's idea into business, writes that conflict can come from our sameness, not only our differences. A peer matters because their life is easy to compare with yours. We do not only notice what peers have. We can begin to use their milestones as a measure of what is possible, important, and on time. That is one reason adulthood can feel more anxious than childhood even as material life improves. The circle of comparison gets sharper.

When winning replaces wanting

This is where desire can become dangerous. At first, the object itself seems to matter: the promotion, the company, or the recognition. But when comparison shapes the desire, relative position can matter more than the thing. You do not only want to build a good company. You want to build one that beats another company. You do not only want wealth. You want the kind that changes where you stand among your peers.

Then desire runs on rivalry instead of purpose, and satisfaction can be hard to reach. Rivalry has no natural endpoint. The people we compare ourselves with change. The meaning of enough shifts with whatever someone else does next. People can then wonder why achievement feels flatter than they expected. Sometimes they have stopped wanting the thing itself and started wanting what it means in comparison with someone else.

The problem is old. The scale is new. Social media makes other people's desires visible all the time. We no longer compare ourselves only with the handful of people around us. We can see a rolling display of people traveling, building, and succeeding in public. We may feel unaffected, but the comparison is available whenever we look.

This is not only a consumer problem. It affects leadership and company building too. Founders can start by solving a real problem and then become preoccupied with another company's valuation. Teams can start by serving customers and later imitate the status rituals of a fashionable company. More choices do not always produce more self-directed lives. They can also give us more chances to copy without noticing.

This is why the topic matters to me. The danger is not only that people chase shallow things. Borrowed desire can look serious. It can even look like courage, because people may be willing to suffer for a script they did not choose. So the answer is not to condemn ambition or want nothing. We learn from other people. We build and become through models. The question is whether we choose those models with our eyes open.

Some models leave us more grounded and free. Others leave us agitated and trapped in performance. Both can look impressive from the outside. The difference is what happens to us as we pursue them.

Cleaner ambition

You probably do not break the loop by force or stop comparing through sheer will. You can change the conditions that shape your desires. Pay attention to whose lives you study most closely. Be more curious about ambitions that grow when a peer succeeds and fade when nobody is watching. Ask better questions. If I achieve this and nobody knows, do I still want it? If the person I compare myself with vanished, would this goal still feel alive? Is this admiration, or is rivalry wearing nicer clothes? Many people do not need less ambition. They need to understand what their ambition is serving.

I do not think we should detach ourselves from desire. Desire animates life. It can create craft, invention, and devotion. The problem is not wanting. It is sleepwalking into wants that other people have installed and we have not examined for ourselves.

We teach one another what matters. Parents, founders, friends, and companies all model not only effort but aspiration. That is one way people spend years climbing toward something and feel strangely absent when they arrive.

I am not exempt. I have wanted numbers because another founder announced them first. Some of the most useful feedback I have received was a version of this essay handed back to me: stop studying other founders so closely, define your own style, and believe in it long enough for it to become yours.

So I keep coming back to a question that helps me think about ambition. Not only what do I want, but who taught me to want this?

Notes and Sources

  • René Girard, Deceit, Desire, and the Novel, 1961, and Things Hidden Since the Foundation of the World, 1978. Mimetic desire; distant versus close models.
  • Luke Burgis, Wanting: The Power of Mimetic Desire in Everyday Life, 2021. Girard applied to business; conflict can come from sameness.

item.title: AI Will Let India Export Consumer Companies
item.description: SaaS helped Indian companies sell software around the world. AI may make it easier for India-born consumer companies to carry operating knowledge across markets.
item.content:encoded:
India's startup imagination was trained on one kind of export: software built in India and sold to the world.

That was not an illusion. SaaS was one of the first categories where Indian startups could build global companies without recreating the whole business in every market. Code traveled. Distribution happened online. Support could be centralized. Product quality mattered more than where the office was. In 2022, Bain described Indian SaaS as second only to the United States in scale and maturity. It also reported that around 20% of Indian SaaS revenue came from India. Companies such as Zoho and Freshworks made the possibility of global software companies built in India easier to see. The advantage was structural: a company could sell its product abroad without exporting the full operating burden.

I believe AI will create a similar opening for consumer companies built in India.

That is not because physical work disappears, logistics stop mattering, or local trust becomes easy. AI may change the cost of carrying operating knowledge across a complex business. That creates room to ask a question that once seemed harder: can a consumer company built in India also serve customers around the world?

Why consumer companies stayed local

A consumer company does not just ship a product. It has to earn trust through many parts of the experience: what it offers, how it prices, how it handles fraud, how it delivers, what it does when something goes wrong, and whether the customer gets a fair resolution. The product is not only the app. It is the whole system the customer meets after pressing the button.

That made consumer companies difficult to take across borders. Entering another market could feel like starting another company. The catalog had to be learned again. Customer language changed. Fraud patterns changed. Local paperwork changed. Much of this knowledge lived in people, meetings, and local managers, rather than in systems everyone could use. As the company expanded, it could lose coherence.

There was an Indian version of this challenge. Companies could sometimes compensate for weak systems by adding people. Labor could cost less, and skilled manual work could patch a broken process for years. In markets with higher labor costs, or fewer people available to do that work, the same approach may not hold. The underlying issue is not simply that consumer businesses involve physical things. It is that operating knowledge is hard to carry and use consistently.

AI lowers the cost of sharing that knowledge

Consumer companies handle a great deal of messy information: support calls, unusual products, payment failures, refunds, inspection results, fraud flags, pricing changes, local rules, and customers who stop converting. The challenge is to turn those signals into useful decisions quickly enough to help the people doing the work.

Traditionally, people have summarized what happened, routed it, escalated it, and explained the pattern to another team. By the time the company acted, the signal could be late or incomplete.

Some parts of this work are changing. McKinsey's work on customer care describes companies using generative AI to analyze call transcripts, summarize conversations, support agents, and identify recurring causes of failure. These examples show work that can be assisted by AI. They do not show that every part of a consumer business is now machine-readable or ready to automate.

AI can help companies compare failure patterns across markets, translate local language, flag pricing outliers, and shorten the time between an event and a decision. The business still needs people to understand the situation and act. The potential gain is better shared context, so the company can learn from an issue in one place and apply that learning elsewhere.

This also changes how we think about India's advantage. If the old path to scale was to add people until the process worked, a new path may be to build systems that help people and agents handle more of the work. That will reward judgment, curiosity, and the ability to use AI well. It does not remove the need for strong operators.

One company, adapted to each market

The opportunity is for more of the business to share its knowledge while local teams adapt the execution. Pricing, support, product quality, and learning could draw on common systems. The last mile would still need to fit each market. The hard part of operating across countries was never copying the app. It was keeping the business from becoming several disconnected companies.

AI can help a company connect what it learns in one place to the work happening elsewhere. A fraud pattern in one market could inform checks in another. A support lesson could help another team respond sooner. The company's knowledge could live in systems that people can use, rather than only in the experience of local experts.

That is the part that resembles SaaS. It is not that software and consumer businesses are the same. It is that both can benefit when a company can coordinate work across distance without rebuilding every capability from scratch.

What India can export next

Some categories could benefit more than others: mobility, commerce, consumer finance, healthcare access, and home services. They combine fragmented operations, trust, and repeated work. Those are areas where better systems for sharing context could make a difference. They may have seemed local because companies had to carry too much knowledge manually. AI may help make some of that knowledge easier to use across markets.

Indian companies also work with varied suppliers, documents, languages, and infrastructure. In the past, that variety could make operations harder to standardize. If companies build systems that can learn from those differences, some of that experience may become useful elsewhere. That is a possibility, not an automatic advantage. Complexity does not become valuable simply because it exists.

This is a thesis, not a result. We are still proving whether a consumer company can share enough operating context through AI to scale across markets without becoming several disconnected businesses. AI will not remove regulatory differences, create trust a company has not earned, fix a poor business idea, or make local execution unnecessary. Companies will still need local understanding, strong operators, category-specific ways to protect customers, and serious attention to regulation.

For years, the exciting question from India was which software company would be built here and sold everywhere. Another question now seems possible: which consumer businesses can use AI to carry what they learn from one market into another? Consumer businesses punish a company quickly when its systems fail in the real world. But if companies can keep learning across markets while adapting to local needs, an India-born consumer company may be able to serve customers globally.

SaaS let India export code. AI will let India build consumer companies for the world.

Notes and Sources

  • Bain & Company, India SaaS Report 2022. Reported Indian SaaS scale and maturity, and the share of revenue from India.
  • McKinsey, "Gen AI in customer care: early successes and challenges," 2024. Examples of generative AI used in customer-care work.

item.title: The EMI Comes Before the Car
item.description: India's used-car market grows when financing makes ownership reachable and lenders can understand the car they are backing.
item.content:encoded:
A used-car buyer does not make just one decision. Often, the first question is how much they can pay each month.

We often talk about India's used-car market as if the main thing it needs is more inventory. Better listings, discovery, inspections, and transfers all matter. But none of them solves the whole problem. Used-car ownership at scale also depends on whether people can finance the car.

A lower price than a new car does not automatically make ownership affordable. A household may be able to manage the car's total price over time, but not pay for it all at once. The question is whether a buyer can turn an aspiration into a monthly payment without putting the family's finances under too much strain. That gap between the price and the cash a household can spend is where the market can widen or stall.

The EMI is the entry point for many buyers

Used cars can help more people enter ownership because their prices may fit a household's budget better. In its July 2025 release, CRISIL Ratings forecast that used-car volume would cross six million units in FY2025-26. It puts the used-to-new ratio at about 1.4 to 1, up from below 1.0 five years ago. CRISIL links the shift to digital adoption, confidence, and better access to finance.

That last point matters. A car may be affordable in total and still be out of reach if buying it uses up a family's cash buffer. Financing can spread the cost over time. For many households, the real question is whether the monthly payment fits without forcing them to give up the money they need for emergencies.

That is why financing penetration matters. On organized platforms, financing now runs above half of purchases, compared with roughly 20 to 25% of the used-car market overall, according to IndianBlueBook. Credit can help make ownership reachable. The lower share across the wider market also shows how many buyers must use savings or wait because financing is not available to them.

The buyer who comes next may want to know the payment before choosing a model. There is another part of the decision that can be hard to see on a spreadsheet. In India, a loan rejection can be socially uncomfortable. A first-time buyer may not want to be told in public that they do not qualify, or that they qualify for less than they hoped.

So buyers may try to find out quietly whether they can get a loan. That creates a problem for a showroom conversation. The seller asks which car the buyer wants and what their budget is. But the buyer may not know their real budget until a lender has assessed the loan.

Until that answer exists, the car search can be only partly grounded in what the buyer can afford. Pre-eligibility can help the customer learn their likely limit and monthly payment before choosing a car. It can make a private question easier to answer, and help the buyer approach the decision with more confidence. It is not only about reducing friction. It is also about giving the customer a clearer choice.

A used-car loan is not just a smaller new-car loan

New-car lending starts with a more standardized asset. The paperwork is usually tidier, residual values can be easier to estimate, and the car has not yet accumulated several owners' histories, repair work, or document gaps. Used cars come with a past that may be difficult to see in full.

Service quality can vary. Accident history may be incomplete. A previous loan may still matter. Transfer may depend on people completing the right steps. A lender has to assess the borrower's ability to repay, the condition and history of the car, and the process around ownership, transfer, and recovery.

If any of those are hard to judge, the lender may offer worse terms, ask for a larger down payment, reject the loan, or require more manual work. In that sense, a used-car loan is an underwriting decision on uncertainty. The lender's view of the car's condition and history affects whether it can judge the risk of lending to the buyer.

A loan can also help a buyer trust the car

A loan provides money, but a lender's decision can also tell a buyer something about the car. A lender's decision may reassure a buyer that the car and its paperwork were assessed for that loan. It is not a warranty, and it does not verify every claim about the vehicle.

That matters in a market where people are still learning how to own a car. But a loan is not proof that every claim about a vehicle is true, and lending itself does not remove every risk. Poorly explained prices or coercive collections can turn ownership into regret. The goal is not more credit at any cost. It is credit built around what the buyer and the asset can support.

The advantage is knowing the asset, not only the cost of funds

Used-car lending is often described as a question of risk appetite. A more useful question is how well the lender understands the car. To lend well, it needs enough information to assess condition, value, title, existing liens, and the steps needed to transfer the car. It also needs a way to manage the asset if the buyer stops paying.

The loan is backed by a car and the facts available about it. A lender that can see more of those facts may make a better decision than one that receives only an application file. A lender connected to reliable vehicle information and operations may be better placed to assess a loan. That advantage depends on the quality of its checks and execution.

Cheaper capital helps, but it cannot fix poor information. If the valuation, document checks, or recovery process is weak, access to cheaper funds can allow bad decisions to grow faster. The harder problem is reducing the gap between what a lender assumes about a car and what is true about it. Better information can give the lender more choices about which funding source should carry each loan.

This is one reason a company close to inspection, pricing, transfer, and recovery could have an advantage as a lender. A standalone lender may receive a file. A lender connected to retail operations could also see how the car was inspected, priced, transferred, and eventually sold. That could give it a fuller picture, provided the information is reliable and used well.

Here are two ways that information could matter. First, details about the car may help a lender check whether the application matches the asset's history. A credit bureau tracks a borrower's repayment history. The car may have its own record, such as service entries and reported kilometers. If the declared kilometers do not fit those records, or other signs do not fit the application, the lender may need to ask more questions.

Differences between an application and a car's records can prompt closer checks. A challan pattern alone does not establish commercial use. Fraud can involve the application, the asset, or both. The lender needs to check the story against the records rather than treat any one signal as proof.

Second, the way a lender handles a car after default can affect the loan decision before default. A standalone lender may have to sell a repossessed car into a market it does not control. A lender connected to a retail operation could potentially inspect, repair, and sell the car through that operation instead.

If that route recovers more, the lender may be able to approve more buyers or offer better terms. But the result depends on what the car actually costs to recover and sell, and what it ultimately fetches. The way out of a loan is part of how the lender judges the loan at the start.

Lending can help build the market it serves

Better inspection and pricing can reduce uncertainty about the car. More reliable information can help lenders make decisions and manage losses. If lending becomes less uncertain, more sources of capital may be willing to fund it. Financing can then help more buyers cross the cash barrier. More financed buyers can improve the market for cars and give lenders more information for future decisions.

That is one path through which lending can help build a market. Financeability is part of market maturity, because buyers and lenders both need enough information to make the exchange work.

If we describe used-car ownership only through listings, inspection, and the retail experience, we see only part of the work. Buyers also need to know whether they can take on the car without exhausting their savings or paying too much because nobody can explain its value. Lending is one of the systems that can help make pre-owned mobility reachable for more people.

Used cars can offer a more affordable way into ownership. Financing affects how many people can take that path.

Notes and Sources

  • CRISIL Ratings, press release, July 2025. Used-car volume crossing six million units, the 1.4x used-to-new ratio (up from below 1.0x), and finance access as a driver of the shift.
  • IndianBlueBook (Mahindra First Choice Wheels), FY25. Used-car financing penetration: above half on organized platforms, roughly 20 to 25% across the whole market.
  • Cars24, Gears of Growth: 2025 Indian Used Car Market Report (our own published consumer research, labeled as such). Financing-first buyer behavior and the pre-eligibility insight.

item.title: Why We Are Not Selling Cars
item.description: The lasting business in mobility is not moving a vehicle once. It is making ownership more certain.
item.content:encoded:
Will the car be what I was promised? Will the transfer finish? If something goes wrong, who will take responsibility?

Those questions are part of what a customer is paying us to answer. Selling the car is one event. Making ownership dependable is the larger business.

In 1960, Harvard professor Theodore Levitt asked a question that many companies still need to answer: What business are you actually in?

His example was the American railroads. They had been giants, then declined. People assumed demand for transportation had fallen. It had not. Cars, trucks, and planes carried that demand instead. The railroads missed the change because, in Levitt's words, "they assumed themselves to be in the railroad business rather than in the transportation business. They were product oriented instead of customer oriented." They defended the thing they sold and lost sight of the need it served.

Mobility companies in India can make the same mistake with cars. We can focus on listing cars better, pricing them better, inspecting them better, financing them faster, and moving more units. Those things matter. But they do not describe the whole job. The car is what the customer sees. Confidence in owning it is what the customer needs.

I do not mean trust as a brand value. I mean confidence in the car, the paperwork, the financing, the transfer, and the help available if something breaks. A transaction happens once. Ownership continues after it. In India, that can mean discovering a challan months later, getting a PUC check, fixing a FASTag that will not recharge, or waiting for an RC to leave someone else's name. People are not only buying a machine. They are buying the hope that owning it will not keep surprising them in ways they cannot manage.

A car is made of thousands of parts that age at different rates. From the outside, a buyer cannot see all of that history. The previous owner may be a stranger. A new car offers one kind of reassurance because it has not yet passed through several owners and repair histories. The used-car opportunity is to make more of that history visible and ownership easier to manage, without making a new car.

That is one way to understand a premium experience in used-car retail. It does not have to mean a fancier showroom. It can mean fewer unanswered questions. A problem that is found, explained, and assigned to someone is easier to deal with than a mystery the customer discovers alone. We are still working toward that kind of experience. It takes systems that connect the details with people who follow through.

The cost of what you cannot see

The used-car category has always had an information problem. Buyers may not know enough. Sellers may not be able to prove enough. Intermediaries often know more than either side. Documents can be messy, vehicle histories incomplete, and condition uneven. So the price is not just payment for the car. It also reflects a guess about what the buyer cannot see.

That uncertainty is one reason inspection, verification, warranties, and return policies matter. They offer reassurance, but each covers only part of the experience. Buyers need to know the vehicle is what it claims to be, that the paperwork and transfer can be completed, that financing reflects the asset fairly, and that ownership will be manageable. If something goes wrong, they need to know where to turn. Solving one part can make a useful feature. Connecting the parts can make the whole experience more dependable.

Consider the same car with a cleaner transfer, a clearer history, and fair financing. The metal has not changed. But the buyer may have more confidence in its price, its resale value, and the decision to buy it. The experience around the car changes how people see the car itself.

The proof is in the parts beyond the sale

Transfer is often treated as administrative work. It is also one of the moments when a buyer or seller finds out whether the system can be trusted. If a previous owner remains legally exposed after a sale, the whole market has reason to feel uneasy. That worry can affect prices, resale, and whether people see used cars as a sound choice.

In 2022, the government created an authorized-dealer framework and a procedure for registered dealers to report vehicle delivery to authorities. This gives those dealers a formal way to notify the system. Buyers and sellers still need a clear process to complete the registration transfer and understand when it is recorded. Public systems help determine what ownership means, so they are part of the customer experience too. The government announcement explains the framework.

Financing shows the same connection. The IndianBlueBook FY25 report puts used-car financing at roughly one quarter of purchases, compared with about three quarters for new cars. A lender needs enough information to judge an asset. Clearer history, sound inspection, and reliable title and transfer processes can help make that possible. The same details that reassure a buyer can also help a lender assess a car. Over time, good records may help more cars become financeable, insurable, and easier to resell.

There is another part of ownership that a business cannot ignore: what happens when a car is involved in a crash or a compensation claim stalls. A company that helps people buy cars cannot make every later problem disappear. But it can take seriously the consequences of putting more people into cars and think about the support and recourse people may need afterward. Safety and help after a sale belong in a complete conversation about ownership.

Why Indian auto is still early

Once we see confidence as part of the product, the size of the opportunity looks different. India is not early in demand. CRISIL's July 2025 release estimated the used-car market at about ₹4 lakh crore and forecast more than six million units for FY2025-26. MoRTH registration data for 2022 put ownership at roughly 35 cars per 1,000 people. IndianBlueBook's FY25 report put the organized share of used-car sales at about a third. The figures point to a large market where many parts of ownership remain fragmented.

Information is uneven. Transfer can still be manual. Financing may reflect uncertainty as much as the car or the buyer. In more developed markets, many systems around buying and owning a car feel routine. In India, parts of that system are still being built.

That is the opportunity. Larger businesses may come from making ownership work more reliably, not simply from listing more cars or moving them faster. The work includes clearer information, cleaner transfer, more understandable pricing, reliable support, and a stronger way to handle problems. As these parts improve, more people may find ownership within reach and resale easier to trust.

I see this as the same question behind several other essays about cars. The market can grow when ownership becomes easier to enter and live with. Lending can widen access when the asset can be understood. An existing car may be a greener choice, but only when its history and condition can be assessed. Road safety is part of the experience people have after they buy. These are connected questions about the systems around a car.

The same idea applies inside a company. We cannot make promises about certainty to customers if information and problems get stuck inside our own systems. A company that wants to earn trust outside has to make it possible for people inside to see what is happening, share what they know, and respond when reality changes.

What business we are in

When people ask what Cars24 is, saying only that we sell used cars misses part of the job. The car is the thing that changes hands. We also need to help people understand what they are buying, complete the paperwork, access fair financing, and find support when ownership brings a problem.

Levitt's railroads had customers, tracks, and trains. But they held on to their definition of the business while transportation changed around them. The need in Indian mobility is not simply to put more cars on the road. It is to make owning one a more understandable and manageable choice. The better we do that, the more useful the market can become for everyone involved.

Notes and Sources

  • Theodore Levitt, "Marketing Myopia," Harvard Business Review, July-August 1960. The railroads-versus-transportation argument, quoted verbatim.
  • CRISIL Ratings, July 2025. Used-car market size, volume, and the used-to-new ratio.
  • MoRTH registration data via Data For India. Roughly 35 cars per 1,000 people.
  • IndianBlueBook, FY25. Organized share of used-car sales and financing penetration.
  • Central Motor Vehicle Rules, 2022 "deemed ownership" amendment.

item.title: We Deleted Every Title Except Builder
item.description: Cars24 changed its old title system. The deeper question is how to give people closer to a problem the context and responsibility to act.
item.content:encoded:
A few months ago I was walking through a refurbishment centre in the evening, after most of the floor had emptied out. One technician was still under a car on a lift, finishing a job another team could have picked up the next morning. His shift had ended. The car was scheduled for early delivery. I asked why he was still there. He said the customer needed the car early because there was a wedding in the family, and he had told the team he would finish it.

I have thought about that answer often. It was not dramatic. It was precise. He saw an open loop and closed it.

That is the kind of work I think a modern company needs more of. Builder does not mean founder, and it does not mean engineer. It means someone who can see what needs to happen and help change the situation. At Cars24, Builder is the shared title. It names the way we want people to work: seeing what needs to happen and helping change it.

The old system rewarded distance

For a long time, companies rewarded people who stood further from the work. They coordinated the people doing it, translated updates for another layer, and gained status as their distance from execution grew. This was not simply because people were bad at their jobs. Context was expensive to gather and share. Large companies needed people to route information, review decisions, and help different parts of the business stay connected.

That is part of the point Jay Galbraith made about organization structure: it helps process information under uncertainty. Over time, we turned distance from the problem into a ladder. The person closest to the customer could sit below the person explaining the customer. The person writing code could sit below the person turning it into a roadmap update for someone who no longer needed to know the code.

That structure was useful in some ways. But the cost of gathering, moving, and acting on context is changing. If people can see the state of a business more directly, and if messy information no longer has to pass through several human summaries, then pure coordination becomes less valuable. It does not become worthless. The person closest to a problem can matter more when they also have the context and ability to act. The technician who finishes the car, the sales operator who calls back when the first answer did not help, and the engineer who fixes a strain before it becomes an outage are doing different jobs. They share a willingness to see the work through.

Responsibility still matters

An argument for Builders can sound like an argument against management. That is not what I mean. Companies still need judgment, standards, coaching, conflict resolution, and choices about where to put resources. People need to know who can make which decisions. What is losing value is coordination theater: chase emails, status decks, and updates reformatted for another layer.

People who take on wider responsibility should help the organization work better. In Flatland, that is stewardship, not higher rank. A Steward carries more responsibility for the whole system. Greater surface area does not give someone greater status. It gives them greater stewardship. People may take temporary authority over a particular problem or decision. That does not create a standing class of leaders.

Titles can still communicate useful information about responsibility and decision rights. But when a title decides who gets context, who gets heard, or whose judgment counts before anyone has looked at the problem, it has become a gate. Strong companies should remove gates that no longer help the work. The customer does not care how elegant the escalation path looked. The customer cares whether the issue was resolved.

Agency means carrying the outcome

A company that values Builders cannot treat work as more important just because it has moved farther from the consequences. If two people close loops that matter, they are doing different work, not holding different kinds of dignity. Many companies say they value ownership but keep rewarding status. People doing essential work can feel that gap before anyone names it.

There is a cost to real agency. If the call was yours and the outcome was poor, you cannot hide behind someone else's decision. The broken version belongs to you too. It becomes harder to say, "It was not my job," even if that is technically true. Carrying the consequence is part of ownership.

Autonomy without responsibility is a slogan. The two come together in practice. Builder is not a motivational label. It describes a way of working with less reliance on permission and more responsibility for what happens next. That can feel energizing. It can also feel difficult. Both responses are real. A company needs to make space for people to learn how to carry that responsibility, with the context and support the work requires.

As coordination gets cheaper, people who can move a problem forward may create more value. AI can help by making context easier to gather and share. The point is not to remove every layer or move every decision outward. It is to place context and authority closer to the problem wherever the work allows, while keeping the structure that protects quality, safety, and coherence.

What changed when the old prefixes went

At Cars24, we removed the old bands, grades, and designations, including vice president, director, and manager. Builder became the shared title. The intended model is a company where people contribute as players in the work, rather than treating their job as supervising someone else doing it.

That does not mean no one takes responsibility for direction, or that every decision is made by everyone. It means that a title should not create a permanent class whose job is to review and rally other people. People take on responsibility for the problem in front of them. When someone needs to care for the health of more of the organization, that work is stewardship, not a claim to higher status.

I say this as someone who had to change my own habits. I started the company to do things with my own hands. As we grew, I became a master delegator and moved further from the work. My days filled with reviews and updates instead of building. AI has made it easier for me to work directly on things again. It can also make that possible for others, if we give them context and room to act.

Builder is the word we chose for that shared responsibility. The test is whether more people can understand the problem, do useful work, and close the loop.

Notes and Sources

  • Jay Galbraith, "Organization Design: An Information Processing View," 1974. Organization structure as a way to process information under uncertainty.
  • Autonauts, Cars24's public culture site. Cars24's public account of its culture and organization model.

item.title: AI Changes the Shape of the Company
item.description: Adding AI to an old workflow can make it better. The deeper change is to rebuild how a company carries context and makes decisions.
item.content:encoded:
Some of the least changed companies I know now call themselves AI-first. Often, they mean they have added AI to support, sales, coding, or search. The workflow may be better. The company itself may be much the same.

Cars24 began as an engineering company. As transactions grew, our attention moved toward operations: inspections, logistics, refurbishment, and financing. I let that happen. The company drifted from the reason it had started. Around 2023, it became clear that the old way would not take us forward. We had to change how the company worked while the live business kept running.

A founder I respect told me recently that his company was AI-first. I asked what had changed. He said they had integrated GPT into support. I asked what else. He paused, then said they were still figuring that out. I do not say this to mock him. Most of us built companies for a world where context was expensive to gather, share, and act on. That is the distinction I care about. An AI-first company uses AI. An AI-native company changes how it works because AI changes what is possible.

A company carries context

That can sound like a small difference until you look at what a company does. In 1937, economist Ronald Coase asked why firms exist instead of buying every task on the open market. He argued that using the market has costs. A firm can reduce them by coordinating work through managers instead. Hierarchy was not simply ego or bureaucracy. It was one way to gather information and coordinate action. Jay Galbraith later described organization design as a way to process information under uncertainty. Mel Conway showed how an organization's communication structure can shape the systems it builds.

A growing company gathers signals from the edges, makes sense of them, and turns them into decisions. Its structure affects who sees those signals, when they see them, and what gets lost along the way. As a company grows, no one person can see the whole system. Layers help summarize what is happening, pass important information upward, and carry decisions back down. That approach helped large organizations stay coordinated. It also added distance and delay.

A layer is a design choice

Every layer can add delay and reduce detail. Facts get polished as they move up. Decisions get simplified as they move down. By the time someone who can act sees the issue, the account may be cleaner but less useful than the reality that produced it.

AI is changing the cost of carrying context. It can summarize, route, sort, and draft an initial analysis. That does not replace judgment. It does mean some work once carried through a chain of people can happen faster and more continuously. The old structure deserves another look.

The question is not whether to use AI. Most companies will. The harder question is what kind of company makes sense when carrying context becomes cheaper. How many layers do we need? Which meetings exist mainly to move information? Which decisions wait because only a few people can see enough to make them? These are questions about how the company works, not which tools it buys. An AI-first company adds software to an old shape. An AI-native company asks whether that shape still serves the work.

In many companies, context travels in batches through meetings, decks, reviews, and escalation chains. People wait for the round trip before they act. Some recurring rituals are there because people do not share enough of the same picture. Status meetings, chase emails, escalation decks, and permission loops often try to solve that same problem. When people can see the situation together, meetings can focus on decisions instead of retelling what happened.

Our monthly P&L review is one example. It used to run for three hours. We began by waiting for someone from business finance to explain how revenue had moved and why the margin had shifted. Now people come in having already asked an agent to read the P&L and answer those questions. The diagnosis happens before the meeting. The meeting lasts half an hour, and most of it goes to what we do next and who owns it. The time in the room has shifted from establishing what happened to deciding what to do.

That is a useful change, but faster meetings alone do not make a company AI-native. If a year of work happens in a month, the business should also learn and improve faster. Otherwise, it may have produced more activity without more progress. I will not call Cars24 AI-native because of the tools we adopted. I will believe the change when we are visibly faster on what matters: customer experience, unit economics, growth, and how quickly we can do new things.

What changes, and what remains human

The lazy version of this argument says AI replaces managers. I do not think that is the right way to describe it. AI can reduce the coordination work around management: collecting status, reformatting updates for another layer, or meeting because no one can otherwise see the same picture. Judgment, hiring, standards, coaching, conflict, and hard calls under uncertainty still need people.

This does not mean every layer or form of authority should disappear. Structure can support accountability, incentives, quality, safety, and coherence. The narrower question is whether a layer still helps the work, or mainly relays information that people could share directly.

The change also depends on how people treat the truth. If people hoard context, soften bad news, or wait for permission because mistakes are punished more than delay, AI will not make the company wiser. It may help produce a polished account of the wrong story more quickly. Cheaper ways to carry context matter only if people can share what is really happening.

Shared context can give more people agency

Traditional organizations often move decisions upward because that is where information collects. An issue from a store goes to headquarters because headquarters has the wider picture. That can be a context problem rather than a character problem. AI may help by making more of the relevant picture available to the people closest to the issue. The goal is not to have more agents. It is to help more people see enough to act.

This is the change I have felt most directly at Cars24. What mattered was not simply adding tools. It was asking which coordination work still needed people and which could now happen directly, with shared context. Many companies will buy new tools and leave their old ways of working in place. They will summarize meetings that could disappear, make reports clearer while keeping decisions far from the work, and call that transformation. It may be useful modernization. It is not the same as changing the company.

Start with the shape

The shape of the company is part of its AI strategy. Start there and the questions change. Which meetings should go? Why does an update pass through three people before anyone acts? If you were building the company today, with AI available from the start, would you choose the same layers, rituals, and distance between signal and action?

If the answer is no, the gap between the company you have and the one you would build is the work of transformation. It reaches into authority, incentives, reporting rhythms, hiring, and status. That work can take years. Anyone who says a company became AI-native in six months should be able to show what changed in how it operates.

A McKinsey survey from 2025 tested 25 factors and reported that workflow redesign had the largest effect on whether companies saw a bottom-line impact from generative AI. That finding is one data point, not proof that every company should redesign in the same way. It does point to a useful question: what changed in the work after AI arrived?

The next decade will not split companies into those that use AI and those that do not. Most will use it. The difference will be between companies that keep their old shape and those that change how context moves, who can act, and how quickly they learn. That is the difference between AI-first and AI-native. One adopts the technology. The other redesigns the company around what the technology makes possible.

Notes and Sources

  • Ronald Coase, "The Nature of the Firm," Economica, 1937. Why firms and hierarchies exist: to reduce the costs of coordinating work.
  • Jay Galbraith, "Organization Design: An Information Processing View," 1974. Structure as a way to process information under uncertainty.
  • Melvin Conway, "How Do Committees Invent?", 1968. How organizations' communication structures can shape the systems they build.
  • McKinsey, "The State of AI: How organizations are rewiring to capture value," 2025. A survey of 25 factors reported workflow redesign had the largest effect on bottom-line impact from generative AI.

item.title: Companies Scale at the Speed They Learn
item.description: Hiring can add capacity, but a company scales well when it can see reality, learn, and change as complexity grows.
item.content:encoded:
Companies scale at the speed they learn. Hiring more people, adding layers, and creating reviews do not guarantee that a company gets better.

It is easy to see why people equate scale with headcount. Industrial businesses grew by adding labor, coordination, and management. When demand rose, the organization expanded to meet it. That model worked well enough to become instinct. Even now, when people say they want to scale, they often mean more output without losing control. When they say they have reached a limit, they may mean the current team cannot carry more complexity.

The familiar response follows: hire, add a layer, create a review, start a meeting, build a dashboard. The company gets bigger, but the system underneath it may not get wiser. It gets heavier. Some organizations look bigger long before they work better.

Headcount is not useless. Talent matters. But scale and capability are different things. A company becomes more capable when it gets better at seeing reality, learning from it, and changing its behavior before complexity becomes drag. Those are outcomes of how the system works, not just how many people it employs. A weak company can double its headcount and stay confused. It can add managers and keep making poor decisions. It can create planning rituals and rediscover the same problems in new forms. People feel busy, but the company does not become clearer.

Look beneath the event

Systems thinking becomes useful when it helps us see what keeps producing a problem. Donella Meadows showed how an event sits within a pattern, which sits within a structure, which rests on assumptions about how the world works. A company may treat each missed sale as a separate surprise. But the recurring cause could be how information moves. A conflict may look like a personality problem when incentives keep people working against one another. A culture may reward concealment until protecting yourself seems more sensible than telling the truth.

A company that keeps improving gets better at finding the level where a problem lives. It learns to tell the difference between a symptom that needs a patch and a structure that needs to change.

The deepest causes are not always visible on an org chart. Many people are comfortable changing plans, measures, roles, and processes. Fewer are comfortable questioning the assumptions underneath them. Yet those assumptions often shape the rest of the system.

Peter Senge described a learning organization as one that can surface its mental models and update them. A mental model is an assumption we use to make sense of the world. This does not mean reading more or running better workshops. It means being able to notice beliefs that have gone untested and ask whether they still fit reality.

Consider beliefs such as: growth matters at any cost; the founder knows best; bad news should be softened before it travels; disagreement means disloyalty. These are not private thoughts once they shape incentives, escalation paths, hiring, and what people feel safe saying. They become part of the system.

Jim Collins tells the story of A&P, which ran an experiment that showed its model was no longer working, saw the result, and shut the experiment down. It is one account of a wider problem. Companies may see evidence and still struggle to act on it. Often, a useful intervention is not a reorganization. It is a clearer view of what is happening and a willingness to change an assumption.

Truth has to move

The phrase I keep coming back to is that truth has to move. That is not a slogan. It is part of the company's operating system. Signals from the edges have to travel inward without being distorted. People need to be able to say, "This is not working," while there is still time to act. Meetings should exist to help people make judgments, not to perform the act of being updated.

Meadows tells a story about a Dutch housing development. Some identical houses had their electric meters in the basement. Others had them in the front hall. The houses with the visible meters used 30 percent less electricity. In the story, the important change was where people could see the information. Nothing else about the houses changed.

Companies also depend on what people can see and say. Fear can slow down information. Defensiveness can change how people describe what happened. Status can affect whose account gets believed. How people work together therefore affects how well a company understands its own problems.

Amy Edmondson's research on psychological safety is relevant here. Psychological safety means people can take interpersonal risks, such as raising a concern or admitting a mistake. Its value is practical: a company needs to hear about a problem while there is still time to respond. This is not a call to avoid discomfort. A company can keep high standards and make it possible to tell the truth about whether those standards are being met.

The founder cannot be the whole learning loop

Founder-led companies can run into a particular limit. In the early years, founders often carry the context, make the calls, and absorb the shocks. That concentration can create speed when the company is small. But if the founder stays at the center of every decision as the company grows, work starts to wait. Information gets edited on the way up. Decisions collect in one place.

It is easy to mistake that for a need for more supervision. Often, the company needs more people who can understand the situation and act within clear decision rights. That means better information flow, local context, and fewer rituals built around permission. The founder cannot remain the entire learning loop. The company has to build the ability to learn across the work.

I lived this one personally. For years, I believed it was my job to come up with the projects for the quarter or year and hand the problem statements to the teams. I have stopped doing that. My job now is direction, not route.

Cars24's vision is better drives, better lives. In a country where many people are buying their first car, and a car can carry family identity and represent one of the largest purchases they make, the ownership experience should be extraordinary. One level down, we have a direction teams can test and debate: increase certainty in an uncertain world.

From there, teams choose the projects. There are many ways to move toward a vision. The people closest to the work can choose better routes than I could assign, though they sometimes choose routes I would not have picked. The discipline is to let those choices run while learning from what happens.

That only works if the learning loop is fast. Leaving direction broad is responsible only when a poor bet becomes visible in weeks, not at the year-end review. Clear direction and fast learning depend on each other.

Learning matters more as complexity grows

AI makes this question more important because it can change how quickly people gather and share context. The gains will depend on how the company learns. If people have useful information and room to act, the company may handle more complexity without adding the same amount of coordination. If the learning system is weak, new tools will not fix that by themselves.

Scale is not just a measure of size. It is also the ability to keep learning as the work becomes more complex. The question is how a company can grow without losing its ability to see what is happening and change course. That asks more of the company than growth or speed alone. It asks whether the company gets more capable as it gets bigger.

Notes and Sources

  • Donella Meadows, "Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System," 1999, and Thinking in Systems, 2008. Leverage points and the Dutch electric-meter story.
  • Peter Senge, The Fifth Discipline, 1990. The learning organization and surfacing mental models.
  • Jim Collins, Good to Great, 2001. The A&P story about seeing evidence and acting on it.
  • Amy Edmondson, "Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams," Administrative Science Quarterly, 1999. Psychological safety and learning behavior in teams.

item.title: What India Must Learn From Its Road Deaths
item.description: Drivers make mistakes. India needs road-safety systems that can see what happened, respond, and learn before the same failure kills again.
item.content:encoded:
There is hardly a family in India without a road-crash story. A father who never came home. A cousin whose leg never healed properly. A child hit outside a school gate. A delivery rider who left the news before his family had recovered.

My story is from 2005. I was at IIT Bombay. One night, a batchmate and I were riding a Kinetic home late through Mumbai. He was driving. I was on the pillion. We did not see a divider in time. The scooter hit it, and he was thrown across the road. I fell on the near side. A taxi ran over him. We picked him up, and I held him in my lap on the way to the hospital. He did not survive. I walked away without a scratch.

What stayed with me was not only grief. It was the unfairness. Same vehicle, same night, same crash. One of us lived and one did not.

That is the place road death occupies in Indian life. It is close enough to wound almost every family, yet familiar enough to feel normal. And because the system is fragmented, it rarely learns.

In 2023, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways recorded 172,890 road deaths, the highest number India has logged. Even that is likely an undercount. The WHO once estimated the true toll at roughly 300,000 in 2016, about twice the official count for that year. The government's Sample Registration System also put 2022 deaths far above the police count. The exact number matters. So does the fact that we still cannot agree on it. When a country cannot count road deaths cleanly, it cannot see the problem clearly enough to learn from it.

We usually talk about the visible causes: speeding, drunk driving, bad roads, missing helmets, weak enforcement. All are real. But they do not explain the deeper failure. That is a failure of trust in the systems around a crash.

I mean trust in a practical sense. Can institutions trust the data they use? Can a bystander help without fearing punishment? Can a family reach the compensation it is owed? Can the engineer, police officer, hospital, and judge work from the same account of what happened? Too often, the answer is no. When a system cannot trust its own picture of a crash, it cannot learn from it.

There is a working example. Piyush Tewari founded the SaveLIFE Foundation after losing a teenage cousin in a crash. The foundation rebuilt a stretch of the Mumbai-Pune Expressway using the Safe System approach. This approach starts from the fact that people make mistakes, even when trained. Roads and emergency systems should be designed so those mistakes are less likely to kill. After more than 3,500 engineering defects were fixed and ambulance response fell from about 35 minutes to under 10, deaths on that corridor fell by roughly half between 2016 and 2020. The lesson is not that drivers there suddenly became better. The system stopped allowing as many mistakes to become fatal.

I did not come to this work from a safe distance. Neither did Amar Srivastava and Deepanshu Gupta, who founded the Indian Road Safety Campaign and built Crashfree India with Gajendra Jangid, my co-founder at Cars24. The last eighteen months of this work have brought the failures close. One pattern keeps coming back: they are connected.

The first failure is memory

Start with the data. India has several road-death systems that do not reconcile: police-based MoRTH and NCRB figures, survey-based Sample Registration System estimates, and the WHO's modeled numbers. The same crash should contribute to one shared picture. Instead, the estimates can differ by more than a lakh of deaths. A wrong baseline makes targets performative and evaluation little more than a guess.

Digitizing paperwork will not fix this by itself. Systems like iRAD and eDAR point in a useful direction. One geo-tagged record is better than several disconnected forms. But digitizing a bad diagnosis still produces a bad diagnosis. If an official is rewarded for closing a file rather than tracing how a crash happened, faster data entry only speeds up poor judgment.

Roads everyone knows are dangerous

The same gap appears on the road itself. Crashfree's Project Rakshak, a youth-led infrastructure effort, works on a part of road safety that formal systems often miss: places locals already know are unsafe, but that authorities may act on only after people are hurt or killed. A blackspot should not have to earn its name through repeated deaths.

By mid-2026, Rakshak teams had assessed more than 120 high-risk locations across 18 cities and secured approvals for fixes at 25. Those sites had likely seen more than a thousand crashes once under-reporting is considered. The planned interventions were expected to reduce crash risk there by a fifth to a half. The point is not only the scale. It is the method: authorities can be shown where roads are dangerous before more deaths force their attention.

The work also found that crash data for these sites was almost certainly undercounted, because non-fatal crashes often disappear from formal records. The road was telling one story. The file was telling another.

After the crash, opacity keeps killing

The same break continues after impact. This is one of the least discussed failures in Indian road safety. India can pass a Good Samaritan law, publish ambulance numbers, and announce compensation schemes. The Good Samaritan protections were set out by the Supreme Court in 2016 and later written into Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act. But when citizens do not know their rights, hospitals respond unpredictably, and families cannot navigate the system, a law on paper does not create trust in practice.

You see the gap in the first minutes after a crash. A crowd gathers. Nobody knows whom to call or what helping the victim might cost them.

That is why even a first-responder card matters. Early Crashfree material reduced roadside action to three words: Check, Call, Care. Make the scene safe, call 112, control bleeding, and start CPR if needed. In a working system, these steps would be clear. In India, that clarity is itself missing infrastructure. Helping someone should not require private courage and improvisation every time.

You see the gap again in trauma care. A visit to the AIIMS Trauma Centre makes the problem concrete. Many serious crash victims still arrive without meaningful care before reaching hospital. Ordinary people, often rickshaw drivers, end up acting as first responders without training or equipment. Even at a leading trauma centre, the chain before arrival is thin.

This is why PM RAHAT, the government's cashless-treatment scheme for crash victims, matters. It provides eligible victims with up to ₹1.5 lakh in cashless treatment for up to seven days under the scheme. Hospitals and police still need to coordinate so a crash victim can get care without delay. The scheme's details set out its limits and eligibility.

Then there is compensation. The law exists, but access is broken. In January 2025, the Supreme Court observed that very few victims benefit from the schemes because public awareness is low and authorities do too little to explain them. A 2021 World Bank study found that only 14% of poor households affected by a crash received any compensation. The financial blow amounted to more than seven months of household income.

Crashfree's field brief, Justice Unserved, describes the system beneath those numbers. Hit-and-run claims are filed for roughly 12% of eligible crashes each year. Seventy percent of surveyed low-income households did not know compensation existed. Nine in ten pending hit-and-run claims are stalled on paperwork. Hundreds of crores remain unclaimed in tribunals, including ₹459 crore in Bombay. The national backlog exceeds ten lakh cases worth more than ₹80,000 crore.

Middlemen step into that gap. Unregulated “ambulance chasers” approach victims at hospitals and offer to handle claims for a commission. In 2021, the Bar Council suspended 28 advocates for filing fake motor-accident claims. When a system is opaque, trust gets privatized and sold back to the victim. India's problem is not only compensation law. It is access to compensation.

Many families do not know how to navigate a compensation claim. They need accessible, case-specific legal help and clear support through the process. A 90-minute awareness session and a printed checklist can help them get started. At helpdesks run inside AIIMS and Sharda Hospital, more than a hundred families queued for that support. This is what opacity looks like up close. People need money, but they also need help understanding the process. Policy says a victim can claim. Trust means the victim knows it, believes it, can prove it, and can stay with the process long enough to receive it.

Nobody owns the chain

The failure to learn is cultural as well as administrative. India still treats road deaths as the natural cost of growth: more vehicles, wider roads, rising fatalities for a while, then a quiet shrug. We have built speed, volume, and aspiration. We have not built a safety system to match them.

One line kept recurring in this work: information is infrastructure. Weak crash data weakens safety design. Hidden hazards weaken prevention. An unclear compensation process weakens access to justice. These failures persist in part because responsibility is divided across transport departments, police, hospitals, local governments, courts, insurers, and ministries. Each can point to its own part and still leave the person on the road inside a failure nobody owns end to end.

That is why India has so much sincere road-safety activity and so little visible outcome. Many people own a piece. Too few are responsible for the full chain.
