A mobility company that wants the upside of the category cannot treat its downside as somebody else's ministry. That is why this work cannot be a CSR sidecar or an awareness week. Any company that benefits from mobility at scale has some responsibility to make the system easier to understand, quicker to respond, or less dangerous. Safety is part of mobility itself.

None of this means Crashfree has solved the problem. It has not. By mid-2026, the work had begun to show another model. Identify dangerous infrastructure before it causes more deaths. Treat compensation as part of justice rather than a legal footnote. Build public tools as well as reports, and use research to help institutions act.

A mature road-safety system assumes people will make mistakes. Its job is to make those mistakes less likely, less severe, easier to respond to, and easier to learn from.

Safer roads do not begin when drivers become perfect. They begin when systems can see, respond, and learn well enough that human imperfection is less likely to be fatal.

Notes and Sources

  • Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, Road Accidents in India 2023. 172,890 deaths, the highest recorded.
  • WHO, Global Status Report on Road Safety 2018, and WHO India. Estimated about 300,000 deaths in 2016 against an official count near 150,000.
  • Sample Registration System estimates via Data For India. About 271,300 road deaths for 2022, far above the police count; the non-reconciling data systems.
  • SaveLIFE Foundation and Piyush Tewari, profiled in Stanford Social Innovation Review. The Mumbai-Pune Zero Fatality Corridor: more than 3,500 engineering defects fixed, ambulance response reduced from about 35 to under 10 minutes, and deaths down about 52% from 2016 to 2020.
  • World Bank, Traffic Crash Injuries and Disabilities: The Burden on Indian Society, 2021. Only 14% of poor crash-affected households received compensation; the burden exceeded seven months of income.
  • Supreme Court of India, S. Rajaseekaran v. Union of India, January 2025. The Court observed that few victims benefit from compensation schemes because awareness is low.
  • Section 134A, Motor Vehicles Act, and SaveLIFE Foundation v. Union of India (2016). Good Samaritan protections.
  • India Legal on unclaimed tribunal funds: ₹459 crore in Bombay, national pending backlog over ₹80,000 crore.
  • Bar Council of India, 2021. Twenty-eight advocates suspended for fake motor-accident claims.
  • Crashfree India public materials: Project Rakshak (more than 120 sites assessed, 25 approvals), Justice Unserved (claim rates, paperwork delays, awareness), the pre-hospital care primer, and legal-awareness helpdesks. These are Crashfree's own published materials.
  • Cars24 H2 FY26 public report. Includes Project Rakshak assessment and approval figures.
  • Project Rakshak live dashboard.

item.title: The Paranoid Survive. The Regulated Thrive.
item.description: Stay alert to the work and steady in yourself. Andy Grove gave us half the sentence. The other half is what helps us keep our judgment.
item.content:encoded:
Most of the worst decisions I have made in more than a decade of building Cars24 came when I was angry, anxious, or stung. I saw the mistake later, after I had cooled down and the decision was already made. The pressure that pushes us to act can also cloud our judgment.

Andy Grove gave us the line many of us live by: only the paranoid survive. I have lived by it. Stay hungry. Move with urgency. Raise the bar, and raise it again once you clear it.

But read Grove closely. His paranoia was not panic. He directed it toward strategic inflection points, moments when a business is about to change, and toward specific fears worth examining. It was a stance he adopted, not a state he lived in. We can miss that distinction. We can turn an instruction to stay alert into a permanent condition of dread. Then the people around us burn out, and our own judgment suffers.

Survival was never the whole point. We want to thrive. Naina Sahni, my coach over the last two years, helped me see that Grove's line needs another half. The paranoid survive. The regulated thrive. The second half is hers. What follows is what I am learning to do with it.

The most demanding team on earth runs cool

These can sound like opposing ideas: push relentlessly, demand more, and never be satisfied; stay calm, stay kind, and look after the people next to you. One example I return to is a rugby team. New Zealand's All Blacks have won more than three quarters of their matches over more than a century, a record few teams in any sport can match. They hold demanding standards and practice a tool called red head, blue head. Red head is tight, panicked, and overwhelmed. Blue head is calm, clear, and accurate. Under pressure, they practice moving from one state to the other.

Their example suggests that high standards do not require people to stay wound up. They can practice how to steady themselves when the pressure rises.

There is evidence that stress affects the brain systems we use to make decisions. Amy Arnsten at Yale has studied how even mild, uncontrollable stress can quickly impair prefrontal cortex function. That area supports judgment, working memory, and planning. Athletes know that effort without recovery has a cost. Training harder without rest does not keep performance rising. It can lead to exhaustion and worse results. A company that stays under pressure all the time can also lose the ability to think clearly.

Feel the emotion. Do not decide inside it.

Regulation is not the softer sibling of ambition. It helps ambition produce better decisions. It starts with a simple discipline: feel the emotion, but do not let it make the decision for you.

We are human. Bad news arrives, someone disagrees, or a plan slips, and we feel it. That is not a flaw we can engineer away. The risk is treating the feeling and the decision as one moment. Daniel Goleman called one version of this an amygdala hijack, when the brain's alarm response takes over before we have time to think. Daniel Kahneman described a related distinction between fast and slow thinking. The work is to create enough space to notice what we feel and consider what to do next.

That does not mean going numb. Antonio Damasio studied people who had lost emotional processing while retaining reasoning abilities. They did not become better decision makers. Some struggled to decide at all. Emotion carries information. Research by James Gross and Oliver John also distinguishes reappraisal, changing how we interpret a situation, from suppression, pushing down the feeling. Suppression does not make the feeling disappear. A useful response is to notice the emotion, consider what it may be telling us, and choose how to act.

Some people hear regulated as a softer word for slow. It can mean the opposite. A composed face that hides bad news is not regulation. It is suppression, and it can make judgment worse. Regulation does not mean feeling less. It means feeling what is there while resisting the urge to let panic choose the next move. The frantic founder and the falsely serene one can make the same mistake. Each lets a feeling determine what the room is allowed to hear.

Compassion helps standards hold

Ambitious people can treat compassion as a reward they give after good performance. I think it helps make good performance possible. Google's Project Aristotle studied what made teams effective. Its findings emphasized psychological safety, the confidence that a person can take an interpersonal risk, such as admitting a mistake, without being humiliated. Amy Edmondson, who studied psychological safety, has said this does not mean being nice at the expense of standards. It means combining care with high expectations. Kim Scott puts it this way: care personally, challenge directly.

A team afraid of humiliation may hide the very risks a vigilant founder needs to understand. Compassion does not require us to lower standards. It can help people meet them while telling us what is going wrong.

Naina describes one part of this with precision. People do not always lie to a frightened person in charge. They calibrate. They soften the truth, wait for a better moment, or take it sideways. The knowledge still exists in the company, but it stops reaching the person who needs to act on it. The person in charge may experience fewer uncomfortable surprises and mistake that for a well-run company. It can be a warning sign.

Calm is trainable, and it can spread

Calm is not simply a temperament we are born with. We can practice how we respond under pressure. I keep a physical trainer and mental coaches close, and use them. My work is not only the hours in meetings and reviews. The hours I spend on my body and mind matter too. That is one place I can practice responding more steadily under pressure.

Our response also affects the people around us. Calm can help others think clearly, while visible panic can make that harder. A team does not simply receive a founder's strategy. It also sees how the founder responds when the news is difficult. A founder who stays open to what is happening can make it easier for others to speak plainly. That does not guarantee the company will stay calm, but it gives the room a better chance to think and act.

I want to stay alert to the work and steady in myself. Hungry without being frantic. Demanding without being cruel. That takes practice. When I get it right, I can face a risk clearly and give the people around me room to tell me what they see.

The paranoid survive. The regulated thrive. I am trying to build for both.

Notes and Sources

  • Naina Sahni. The second half of the sentence comes from her, as does much of my education in it.
  • Andy Grove, Only the Paranoid Survive, 1996. Strategic inflection points; paranoia as aimed vigilance.
  • Ceri Evans, Perform Under Pressure, 2019, and James Kerr, Legacy, 2013. The All Blacks' red head / blue head model. Win record: 500 wins in 652 tests since 1903, the first rugby nation to 500.
  • Amy Arnsten, “Stress signalling pathways that impair prefrontal cortex structure and function,” Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2009. Research on how stress affects prefrontal function.
  • Daniel Goleman, Emotional Intelligence, 1995. The amygdala hijack, building on Joseph LeDoux's fear-pathway research.
  • Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow, 2011. System 1 and System 2.
  • Antonio Damasio, Descartes' Error, 1994. Patients without emotional processing can have difficulty making decisions.
  • James Gross and Oliver John, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2003. Reappraisal and suppression as different emotion-regulation strategies.
  • Google's Project Aristotle, building on Amy Edmondson, Administrative Science Quarterly, 1999. Psychological safety as a factor in team effectiveness.

item.title: The Greenest Car May Already Exist
item.description: Keeping existing vehicles useful can reduce the need for new manufacturing, but reuse only works when buyers can trust the vehicle and its history.
item.content:encoded:
If you care about climate in Indian mobility, you should care about reuse.

New EVs matter, and manufacturing should keep improving. But one near-term lever is making the vehicles that already exist trustworthy enough to stay useful for longer.

Architects have a saying: the greenest building is the one already built. In Indian mobility, the greenest car is often the one already built, when it can safely meet the next owner's needs. The climate comparison still depends on how long it remains useful, what replaces it, and how that replacement is made and driven.

Used carelessly, the line can sound like a slogan. I mean it as a question about how the market works. Every new car uses energy, water, minerals, transport, and manufacturing before anyone turns the key. If usable cars are retired early, distrusted without good evidence, or priced badly, some of that manufacturing is wasted. Reuse can become part of mobility infrastructure, but India still treats it as a fallback.

The climate arithmetic is the easy part

A car's carbon cost begins before it is driven. The IEA estimates that manufacturing accounts for roughly a fifth of a conventional car's lifetime emissions. For an electric car, the upfront amount is higher. The ICCT's 2025 lifecycle study estimates that producing a battery EV emits about 40% more than producing a petrol car, mostly because of the battery. In that study, the EV makes up the difference after roughly 17,000 kilometers. Over its lifetime, it emits about 73% less on Europe's electricity mix. The advantage depends on the grid. The ICCT's India analysis estimated a 19 to 34% lifetime advantage for cars sold in 2021, with that advantage rising as the grid gets cleaner.

The electricity used to charge an EV also changes its lifetime emissions. A result for Europe's grid cannot simply be applied to India. But a lifecycle comparison does not by itself prove that every existing car is a better choice than every new one. The vehicle's condition, remaining life, use, and replacement all matter.

That changes the question. Once a vehicle exists, we should ask not only whether a newer one is cleaner per kilometer. We should also ask whether the current one can keep doing useful work and avoid some new manufacturing. Peer-reviewed lifecycle research supports the idea that extending a vehicle's life can lower its life-cycle CO2 by spreading manufacturing emissions over more years and kilometers. Reuse delays new production. Repair can preserve the carbon already spent. Better diagnosis may help prevent premature scrappage. It can be a quicker lever than waiting for the whole fleet to turn over, though the actual benefit depends on what happens next.

Reuse only works when buyers can trust it

This is where the climate story can become too neat. People say buying used is greener than buying new. It may be, but buyers still need to trust the vehicle, its inspection, its paperwork, and its resale value. If they cannot, they may walk away. Reuse only delivers a climate benefit when it works in the real market.

India still scraps by age, not condition

Policy can make that harder. Delhi-NCR's age-based rules have changed in scope. In December 2025, the government reported protection from coercive action on age grounds for BS-IV and newer vehicles, while older standards were treated differently. Other pollution restrictions still apply. Age alone remains a rough measure of a vehicle's condition.

The intent is understandable. Old vehicles can be highly polluting, and a vehicle that fails a fair fitness test should go. But age is a rough proxy for condition. If a vehicle can be assessed on its actual fitness, emissions, and history, policy can make decisions with better information. Extending the life of a healthy car may avoid new manufacturing. The case is especially relevant for the petrol and diesel cars that make up nearly all of India's fleet today, as well as the EVs arriving now.

Used EVs make the trust problem visible

The point is especially clear with electric vehicles. India's used-EV challenge is often described as a demand, charging, or awareness problem. Those issues matter. There is also a basic difficulty in valuing the battery. Buyers, lenders, insurers, and manufacturers may each use different assumptions about its condition. When the battery's health is hard to assess, buyers may discount the whole vehicle. Lenders may be cautious. Useful EVs may become harder to sell, which can weaken confidence in adoption. A resale problem can become a climate problem.

Battery records are part of EV infrastructure

For years, India's EV conversation has focused heavily on charging. Charging matters. So does knowing what condition a used battery is in. NITI Aayog puts the battery at 35 to 40% of an EV's bill of materials, making it the most expensive part of the car. Yet battery state of health is not a widely accepted, portable measure that everyone can trust.

The available data can reassure, but it does not settle the question for any one car. Geotab's analysis of more than 22,700 electric vehicles across 21 models found average battery degradation of about 2.3% a year. Fast charging above 100kW averaged up to 3.0% a year, compared with about 1.5% for lower-power charging. Heat independently added about 0.4 percentage points a year. These fleet results do not guarantee any individual car's battery capacity after eight years.

A reassuring average is not the same as a comparable test for a particular battery. TÜV SÜD says there is no single accepted method for measuring battery health, and different methods can diverge by up to seven percentage points on the same battery. When the number itself is hard to compare, buyers and sellers have to negotiate around uncertainty.

The answer will not come from advertising alone. It needs standards for battery health, a portable record of each battery, clear warranty status, and a consistent way to recertify a pack. This work has started. India's Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser has issued draft guidelines for a Battery Pack Aadhaar system. It would give each pack a unique Battery Pack Aadhaar Number to track its origin, health, and second life. The EU's Digital Battery Passport is due to become mandatory for EV batteries there from 2027. What remains is implementation that helps a buyer assess a used vehicle. A buyer should not have to interpret a battery through hearsay.

Policy and financing shape whether reuse works

Policy can make reuse easier or harder. If ownership transfer is painful, resale suffers. If road tax makes it costly to move a vehicle across states, buyers have fewer options. Tax can tilt the market too, but the bases matter. GST is 5% on a new EV and 18% on a dealer's margin when an organized dealer resells a used EV. Those rates apply to different amounts, so they are not like-for-like comparisons. A private person-to-person sale outside GST is not inherently a grey-market sale. The GST Council's press release explains the used-EV treatment.

Financing adds another barrier. An ADB and NITI Aayog report reports that EV loans can have 10 to 30% lower loan-to-value and 6 to 18 months shorter tenors than petrol-car loans. Used EV terms are lower still, with battery uncertainty adding to the challenge. The buyer ends up carrying some of the cost of uncertainty.

Warranty transfer is often technically possible, but the process can be buried in brand-specific rules. It should be easy to see whether a warranty transfers and what it covers. Insurance needs ways to value the vehicle that account for battery condition. Finance needs a way to price a well-understood asset with more confidence. None of this is glamorous. It affects whether a second-hand EV feels understandable enough to buy.

Reuse also opens the door to mobility

In India, a used vehicle is often how ownership begins. In a first-time ownership market, a pre-owned car is not just a cheaper option. It can be an entry point. If used vehicles are hard to trust, people who might otherwise buy one can delay or stretch their finances. That makes it harder to expand access while making better use of existing vehicles.

A mature mobility system would help people use existing vehicles for longer when that is safe and useful. That takes enough confidence in a vehicle's condition and history for a second or third owner to make a sound decision. India is still building that confidence.

Climate work includes better information

The climate benefit of reuse depends on ordinary market decisions. A vehicle that stays useful may delay some new manufacturing. Battery information that supports a fair price may keep an EV from being discarded or stranded too soon. Policy that reduces transfer and tax friction may make it easier to find a buyer. These are possible benefits, not a guarantee that every reused vehicle has a lower footprint.

Markets can waste assets when they cannot measure them well. That is true of used cars, and especially used EVs, where an unclear battery can make buyers discount the whole vehicle. Much of the work is practical: better inspection, a consistent battery-health measure, portable warranty information, simpler transfers, insurance that reflects the asset, and financing that can assess risk more clearly. A reused car or EV needs to be clear enough for a buyer to choose without feeling they are gambling blind.

India will not decarbonize mobility only by building new vehicles. It can also make better use of vehicles already built, when their condition, use, and next owner make that the better choice.

Notes and Sources

  • IEA. Manufacturing accounts for roughly a fifth of a conventional car's lifetime emissions; lifecycle tooling at the EV Life Cycle Assessment Calculator.
  • Carl Elefante. The built-environment line this essay adapts: the greenest building is one already built.
  • ICCT, Negri and Bieker, “Life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions from passenger cars in the European Union,” July 2025. BEV production emissions about 40% higher than petrol, the roughly 17,000 km payback, and roughly 73% lifetime advantage on the EU grid.
  • ICCT, global lifecycle assessment of passenger cars, July 2021. The 19 to 34% lifecycle advantage estimated for EVs registered in India in 2021, rising with grid decarbonization.
  • Kagawa et al., “Role of Motor Vehicle Lifetime Extension in Climate Change Policy,” Environmental Science & Technology. Research on vehicle-life extension and lifecycle CO2.
  • National Green Tribunal (2015) and Supreme Court of India (2018) orders on vehicle age in Delhi-NCR. For the December 2025 update on BS-IV and newer vehicles, see the government announcement.
  • Geotab, battery health study, January 2026. About 2.3% average annual degradation across more than 22,700 EVs and 21 models. High-power charging was associated with roughly twice the degradation of lower-power charging; hotter climates added about 0.4 percentage points annually.
  • TÜV SÜD. No standardized method for battery state of health; methods diverge by up to about seven percentage points.
  • NITI Aayog EV supply-chain analysis. Battery pack at 35 to 40% of an EV's bill of materials.
  • ADB and NITI Aayog, EV financing report. EV loans can run 10 to 30% lower loan-to-value and 6 to 18 months shorter tenor than petrol equivalents.
  • GST Council, December 2024. 18% GST on a dealer's margin for used EVs; 5% GST applies to the full taxable value of a new EV. These are different tax bases. See the GST Council's press release.
  • Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser, Government of India. Draft guidelines for the Battery Pack Aadhaar (BPAN) system.
  • EU Battery Regulation. Digital Battery Passport mandatory for EV batteries from 2027.

item.title: The Second-Owner Decade
item.description: India's next ownership wave may be built through used cars, reliable transfers, and support that makes ownership easier to enter.
item.content:encoded:
India's next decade of car ownership will be built in large part through second owners. It will not simply follow the path rich countries took.

That growth will not begin with every household buying a new car through a familiar system. It will not depend on perfect paperwork, easy resale, confident first-time buyers, or ownership habits passed down through generations. Many Indian buyers are still learning what it takes to own a car.

That is not a reason to expect less from the market. It is a reason to understand what needs to become easier. The common story says demand is obvious and the systems around it will catch up later. I think the order can work the other way. More people can enter ownership when the system makes the risks easier to understand and manage.

India is still a first-time ownership country

In developed markets, many people grow up around cars and enter adulthood knowing the basic routines. Insurance, servicing, registration, resale, breakdowns, and renewals may be annoying, but they are familiar. A customer is often replacing a car they already know how to own.

In India, many buyers are entering ownership for the first time. IndianBlueBook found that a used car was the first car owned by 64% of non-metro buyers. That changes what the purchase means.

The fear is not only that a dealer might cheat the buyer. That is a real concern. There is also the worry of not knowing how to manage a car after buying it. What if I make an expensive mistake? What happens when the insurance expires, a challan appears, the FASTag stops working, or the transfer gets stuck?

Buying a first car is not like making a routine purchase. It is closer to trying something unfamiliar with real consequences. You might trust the seller and still wonder what you will do when the first problem arrives. A good buying experience matters, but it cannot remove that uncertainty on its own. The customer also needs to feel able to manage what comes next.

Ownership support is part of trust

People often treat insurance renewal, PUC reminders, service scheduling, challan discovery, FASTag, and RC paperwork as services that come after the main transaction. They may be seen as convenience or as another source of revenue.

For someone new to ownership, these are moments when the experience can either build confidence or add to the worry. Buy a car and then get clear help with the next problem, and the next form may feel less intimidating. A renewal may feel manageable. The car can become part of life instead of a source of constant vigilance.

That confidence grows through ordinary interactions. The insurance is handled. A challan is found and resolved. Service is booked without confusion. Over time, a customer may trust not only the seller but also their own ability to be an owner. Ownership can move from unfamiliar, to manageable, to normal. A market can grow as more people make that journey.

The second-owner decade

This is why India may not become a mass car-owning country by copying a new-car-first path. Used cars can help people enter ownership at a cost that fits their lives better.

India's ownership market has already changed, and it still has far to go. India has roughly 35 cars per 1,000 people, compared with more than 800 in the United States. CRISIL's July 2025 release valued the used-car market at about ₹4 lakh crore and forecast more than six million sales in FY2025-26. According to CRISIL Ratings, that is about 1.4 used cars sold for every new car. The ratio is roughly 2.5 in the United States and 4.0 in the United Kingdom.

The used market is already larger than the new one in India, while still having room to grow relative to those US and UK markets. At the same time, India recorded 4.3 million new passenger vehicles in FY2024-25. Used cars give households another way into ownership without taking on the full cost of a new vehicle. They may also give a first-time buyer a more manageable starting point. People need aspiration, but they also need an entry point they can afford and understand.

Lower prices alone do not make ownership easy. A used-car market also needs reliable systems for the handover, the money, and the months and years after the sale.

Transfer decides legitimacy

One mistake in Indian mobility is to treat transfer as a small administrative detail. RC transfer helps determine whether buying a used car feels legitimate or risky. CRISIL notes that the average used car changes hands at around 3.7 years old. Ownership is therefore a recurring cycle of handovers, not a single event.

If a previous owner remains legally exposed after a sale, insurance continuity is unclear, NOCs are difficult, or state systems rely on manual steps, the market can remain anxious even when demand exists. Buyers and sellers need to know when responsibility has moved from one person to another.

In 2022, the government created an authorized-dealer framework and a procedure for registered dealers to report vehicle delivery to authorities. This gives those dealers a formal way to notify the system. Buyers and sellers still need a clear process to complete the registration transfer and understand when it is recorded. The government announcement explains the framework.

A transfer-heavy market cannot grow on aspiration alone. It needs clear, workable ways to make ownership legitimate for the next person.

Community memory is infrastructure too

There is another kind of infrastructure that does not look like infrastructure: community memory. Team-BHP has become one of the places where people share and preserve knowledge about owning cars in India. It is often called India's Reddit for cars, but that description misses what makes the community useful: no car advertisements, no paid placements, strong moderation, searchable archives, and standards that help knowledge stay useful over time.

The archive holds practical experience. People can learn which cars age badly, which service centres disappoint, what maintenance costs, what holds value, what owners regret, and what they would buy again. A new buyer can use that shared knowledge before making a decision. The experience of previous owners becomes part of what the next owner can see.

The community can also put reputational pressure on a company. Years ago, a group of bikers said a Kawasaki dealer took their money and delivered no bikes. They posted their accounts on Team-BHP instead of going to court. FactorDaily reported that Kawasaki took the loss and delivered the bikes within 45 days rather than risk its reputation on the forum.

That story shows how a public record of customer experience can shape a company's response. In a market where many people are learning ownership as they go, shared knowledge can help reduce the information gap before a platform enters the transaction.

Why the opportunity is larger than commerce

Seen this way, the market is about more than dealerships or listings. It is also about making car ownership easier to understand and trust across the country.

That work touches the whole experience. Discovery can help buyers compare their choices. Financing can open access. Transfer can make a handover legitimate. Service can help an owner deal with problems. Information can make a car's history and condition easier to understand over time.

The market still has room to become easier to navigate. Only about a third of used-car sales run through organized players. About a quarter of used cars are bought on a loan, compared with roughly three quarters of new cars. These are different kinds of gaps, but both point to parts of the market that remain hard to navigate.

The shift is structural, not a short-lived trend, according to CRISIL's Anuj Sethi. He said the rising ratio of used to new cars "signals a structural shift, driven by rising consumer confidence and digital adoption." Confidence matters because parts of car ownership are still manual, fragmented, mistrusted, or intimidating. There is room to build institutions that help people through the full experience, not just complete a transaction.

What actually grows the market

Ask what will grow India's car market and the answers are familiar: higher incomes, more financing, more supply, better roads, and more choice. All can help. The market can also grow when ownership becomes easier to live with.

That means first-time buyers should not feel that one wrong decision will punish them for years. Resale should not feel like a legal gamble. Paperwork should work like a path through the process, not another obstacle. These changes can give people more agency. They can help a buyer understand the decision and handle the responsibilities that come with it.

I believe India's next decade of ownership will be built through second owners, repeated transfers, and greater confidence. The future is not only about having more cars. It is also about helping more people feel ready to own one.
